newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi risks his fate to save Albania force.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi risks his fate to save Albania force.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi put his future on the line on Wednesday after a hard-left mutiny forced him into a humiliating admission that he could not command a parliamentary majority on policy towards Albania.

Addressing the lower Chamber of Deputies, he said he would ask President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro to decide his fate if key ally Communist Refoundation failed to back him in a vote to deploy an Italian-led security force to the Balkan state.

Refoundation, without which the centre-left government cannot muster a majority in the lower house, confirmed it would vote 'no' to the 6,000-strong force of up to eight nations, the first of its kind to be led by Italy.

Its stance compelled Prodi to rely instead on the main centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance to support the mission on the basis of an agreed joint resolution that looked certain to be approved in a vote scheduled for around 1800 GMT.

"I declare now that if the dissent expressed by the Communist Refoundation group persists, I will go immediately to the head of state to inform him officially of the situation and await his evalution," Prodi said.

Options open to Scalfaro, the supreme arbiter in Italian politics, include asking Prodi to tender his resignation or, more likely, sending him to parliament for a confidence vote to determine whether his 11-month-old government stands or falls.

The split has highlighted the vulnerability of Prodi's coalition to Refoundation's casting votes on a difficult domestic agenda, including a drive to reduce social spending to prepare Italy for Europe's planned single currency.

Refoundation says it will back Prodi in any confidence vote as long as it is not on Albania but coalition party leaders now want a thorough review of the stormy alliance to assess whether the hard left can be brought into line on key economic policies.

"What we have to do now is seek a confidence vote on the government's programme. The vote must be on precise issues and not general matters," said Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, leader of the centrist Italian Renewal party.

The opposition supports the Albania force but, sensing an opportunity to embarrass the premier, exacted a high price for voting with the government, insisting Prodi acknowledge that his parliamentary majority has been cut to shreds on the issue.

Prodi took steps to meet the demand in his speech, noting that a Refoundation 'no' vote in the Senate (upper house) on Tuesday, when the government's own majority was enough to get its motion through, had shown he had problems.
"These problems...will become even clearer if, as possible, the Communist Refoundation group were also to vote against the government's recommendations in this house," Prodi said.
Maurizio Gasparri, of the hard-right National Alliance, said the turmoil demonstrated that the government was "brain dead".
"You are making the country look ridiculous. You cannot pretend that your majority hasn't dissolved," he said.

Refoundation regards the Albania force as a neo-colonialist venture and says Italian soldiers will face unacceptable risks. The mission coincides with the 58th anniversary this week of the occupation of the country by pre-war Fascist Italy.
"If the government calls a confidence vote that has nothing to do with the Albania mission, then we'll vote 'yes,'" Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said.
"Our position is still 'no' regarding the mission but we would say 'yes' to anything that has to do with guaranteeing the continuity of the government," he said.
